extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Strategies and structural rules for writing elementary mathematical proofs (case proofs, proofs of disjunctions, existential and uniqueness proofs, using quantifiers and givens). Aimed at teaching how to organize scratch work and final proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break a proof into cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proof can be broken into cases at any time, as long as the cases exhaust all of the possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose cases that are exhaustive (e.g., even vs odd). Cases need not be suggested by a given of the form P ∨ Q; you may invent cases during scratch work. Present each case separately and combine conclusions at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a disjunction P ∨ Q by cases (assume ¬P)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is true, then P ∨ Q is true, so you only need to worry about the case in which P is false. Transform the problem by adding ¬P as a new given and changing the goal to Q. This is equivalent to proving ¬P → Q since P ∨ Q and ¬P → Q are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of final proof: assume ¬P and prove Q. Alternatively, reverse roles and assume ¬Q to prove P. Use this when no natural P/Q cases are suggested. Scratch work may record this transformation before writing the final proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: To use a given of the form P ∨ Q (disjunctive syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are also given ¬P, or you can prove that P is false, then you can use the given P ∨ Q to conclude that Q is true. Similarly, if given ¬Q you can conclude P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when you have both a disjunction and the negation of one disjunct to deduce the other; treat this as a legitimate rule of inference in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing cases via truth of a proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A helpful way to break a proof of P ∨ Q into cases is to assume P in case 1 and assume ¬P in case 2; these cases are exhaustive because P is either true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In case 1, the goal P ∨ Q holds immediately. In case 2, you must prove Q. This reframing often simplifies disjunction proofs and mirrors proving ¬P → Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a universal statement ∀x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a universally quantified statement, start by letting x be an arbitrary object of the domain and then prove P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state 'let x be arbitrary' and avoid assuming special properties of x. Use this pattern repeatedly (e.g., let y be arbitrary) when nested universals appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a universal given ∀x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: To use a given of the form ∀x P(x), plug in a particular value for x (choose a clever substitution if needed) to obtain an instance P(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully choose the term to substitute so that the instantiated fact helps advance the proof (examples in the text show plugging in previously chosen names or constructed objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving an existential statement ∃x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x P(x) you should find (construct or identify) a particular value of x (a witness) and prove P(x) for that object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch work can show how the witness was discovered (e.g., by solving an equation); the final proof exhibits the witness and proves the property succinctly without the scratch-work reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving for the witness via algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the existential claim arises from an equation (e.g., find y with 2y/(y+1)=x), solve the equation for the unknown to produce a candidate witness (here y = x/(2 − x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the algebraic derivation in scratch work; in the final proof present the witness and verify it satisfies the required property. Note division steps are valid only if denominators are nonzero (use given hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving uniqueness: show ∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that an object with property P is unique, show that any two objects y and z that both satisfy P must be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: let y and z be arbitrary, assume P(y) and P(z), then deduce y = z. Use this as the standard form of the uniqueness half of an existence-and-uniqueness proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove ∃!x P(x) (existence and uniqueness strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ∃!x P(x): Prove ∃x P(x) and ∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the two parts existence and uniqueness. Prove existence by exhibiting a witness; prove uniqueness by the two-variable implication above. Alternatively prove an equivalent form ∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative formulations of ∃!x P(x) and strategy choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Several formulas are equivalent to ∃!x P(x) (e.g., ∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)), ∃x∀y(P(y) ↔ y = x), ∃x P(x) ∧ ∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z)). Any of these can guide a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most common technique: prove the third form (existence and uniqueness separately). When using the first form, provide a witness and then show any P(y) implies y equals that witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given ∃x P(x) (existential instantiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a given of the form ∃x P(x) by choosing a name (e.g., x0) for some object satisfying P(x0) and then proceed using P(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that x0 stands for some particular but arbitrary witness guaranteed by the existential; do not assert properties beyond P(x0) unless derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a given ∃!x P(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat ∃!x P(x) as two givens: ∃x P(x) and ∀y∀z((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z). Use the first to instantiate a witness name and the second to conclude equality when two P-objects are encountered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This splits the uniqueness-existence content explicitly and provides a practical way to employ the given in proofs (choose x0 for existence; use the universal uniqueness clause when needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence proofs: reduce work by chaining implications
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving several statements are all equivalent, it is often easier to prove a cycle of implications (e.g., 1 → 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1) rather than every pairwise biconditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the number of conditional proofs required. Label parts of the proof (e.g., 1→2, 2→3, 3→1) and treat each as a separate conditional proof using earlier strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and presentation: scratch work vs final proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Scratch work is used to discover strategies (e.g., trying values, solving for witnesses), but the final proof should present only the logical steps needed to justify the claim without the exploratory reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scratch work to find cases or witnesses; in the formal write-up present the chosen cases/witness and concise verification. Indicate when intermediate transformations (like equivalent forms of statements) motivate strategy choice, but avoid including unnecessary trial calculations.
